reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Nathan and Oski's Haematology
clinicalPearls: Recognise the classic triad: megaloblastic anaemia, diabetes mellitus and progressive sensorineural deafness, all presenting in infancy or early childhood
Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC19A2, encoding high-affinity thiamine transporter 1 (THTR1)
The megaloblastic anaemia does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, but does respond to pharmacological thiamine supplementation
Thiamine treatment can correct the anaemia and improve glycaemic control, though it usually does not reverse the sensorineural hearing loss
The bone marrow shows megaloblastic changes and often ringed sideroblasts
Diabetes is typically non-autoimmune and may become insulin-dependent over time
Additional features can include optic atrophy, retinal changes, cardiac defects and short stature
Lifelong thiamine supplementation is required; interruption can allow anaemia and hyperglycaemia to recur
reference.pathophysiology: Rogers syndrome results from loss of function of the high-affinity thiamine transporter THTR1 encoded by SLC19A2. Cells that depend heavily on this transporter for thiamine uptake, notably haematopoietic precursors, pancreatic beta cells and cochlear cells, become thiamine deficient at the intracellular level despite normal systemic thiamine. Impaired thiamine-dependent enzyme activity (including transketolase and the pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes) disrupts nucleic acid ribose synthesis and energy metabolism, producing megaloblastic dyserythropoiesis, beta-cell failure with diabetes, and cochlear degeneration with deafness. Supraphysiological thiamine can drive residual low-affinity transport and restore intracellular thiamine, correcting the haematological and metabolic features.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemia
Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome and other mitochondrial disorders
Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) given diabetes with deafness
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing macrocytic anaemia
Bone marrow examination for megaloblastic change and ringed sideroblasts
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin for diabetes
Ophthalmological and echocardiographic assessment for associated anomalies
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring transfusion in an infant
Cardiac decompensation from associated structural defects
reference.prognosis: Thiamine supplementation typically corrects the anaemia and improves diabetes control, but sensorineural deafness is usually irreversible and lifelong treatment with monitoring is needed to maintain remission.
pitfalls: Treating the anaemia with B12 or folate and concluding the marrow is unresponsive
Failing to link the anaemia, diabetes and deafness as one syndrome
Stopping thiamine once counts normalise, allowing relapse
Missing the diagnosis in a child labelled as having early-onset diabetes alone
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Start and continue lifelong high-dose thiamine supplementation, which drives residual low-affinity transport to correct the anaemia and improve diabetes control
Recognise that the anaemia does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate, so thiamine is the specific treatment
Treat the non-autoimmune diabetes with insulin as it becomes insulin-dependent, adjusting as thiamine improves early glycaemic control
Provide hearing aids or cochlear implantation for the progressive sensorineural deafness, which is usually irreversible
Monitor the full blood count, glycated haemoglobin and hearing, and screen for associated cardiac and ophthalmological anomalies
Offer genetic counselling and testing for biallelic SLC19A2 variants, with screening of at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
